sentences.text: Helicoprion is primarily known from its unique fused, spiral-shaped tooth whorls, which resemble a circular saw.

Most fossils consist of a spiral-shaped root holding dozens of enameloid teeth arranged in a logarithmic spiral, and CT scans of the best-preserved specimen revealed nearly complete upper and lower jaws preserved in three-dimensional articulation.
The animal had a skeleton made of cartilage like other chondrichthyan fish, and skull characteristics confirm that Helicoprion belongs to the chondrichthyan subclass Holocephali.

Helicoprion jaws were extensively laterally compressed, though this may be partly due to fossil compression artifacts, while the upper jaw was lined with small, low, rounded teeth that formed a pavement scraping against the main tooth whorl. The labial cartilage wedged into the upper jaw to distribute forces and limit jaw closure.
Tooth-like scales called odontodes have been found associated with Helicoprion bessonowi fossils in Kazakhstan.
The largest known Helicoprion tooth whorl, IMNH 49382, measured 56 cm in diameter and 14 cm in height, belonging to an individual at least 7 meters long.
The first known Helicoprion specimen preserved a partial tooth whorl with 15 teeth, 14 of which are visible.

A 2015 biomechanical study suggests Helicoprion's spiral teeth had different functions based on their position in the whorl, where the front teeth snagged prey, middle teeth speared it, and hind teeth punctured it to push it into the throat.
The genus Helicoprion was first described by Alexander Karpinsky in 1899.
Hay described the species Lissoprion ferrieri in 1907 and 1909 based on fossils found in phosphate deposits along the Idaho–Wyoming border.
More than half of the Helicoprion fossils belong to the species H. davisii, primarily found in the Phosphoria Formation in Idaho.

The sharp teeth of Helicoprion imply that these animals were carnivores, and its diet likely consisted primarily of cephalopods like belemnoids, nautiloids, and ammonoids, and it may have also hunted cartilaginous and unarmored bony fish.
The saw-like tooth arrangement and lack of tooth wear suggest Helicoprion ate soft-bodied prey rather than hard-shelled organisms.

During feeding, Helicoprion squeezed prey between its tooth whorl and the palatoquadrate bones, likely capturing prey with rapid jaw closures and then using repeated opening and closing motions to saw through it.
Studies suggest the tooth whorls were located in the lower jaw and used for grasping and slicing soft-bodied prey like cephalopods.
The type species of the genus Helicoprion is Helicoprion bessonowi.
Helicoprion belongs to the extinct order Eugeneodontiformes within the clade Holocephali, which today only includes chimaeras, an order that lived from the Devonian to the Triassic periods.
Naugolnykh and Naumkin proposed in 2018 and 2023 that Parahelicoprion might be a junior synonym of Helicoprion, though some authors continue to consider Parahelicoprion distinct from Helicoprion.
Helicoprion lived during the Cisuralian to Guadalupian stages of the Permian period, approximately 290 to 270 million years ago.
Based on fossil locations, it is speculated that Helicoprion species lived along the southwestern coast of Gondwana and later that of Pangea.

Charles R. Eastman challenged Karpinsky's classification of H. davisii in 1902, placing it in the genus Campyloprion, but concluded in 1903 that Campyloprion was similar enough to Helicoprion to be reassigned as a lineage within that genus.
Eastman supported the hypothesis that the whorl was a defensive structure on the body rather than part of the mouth, despite similarities to other chondrichthyan teeth.
A hypothesis suggests Helicoprion fed on ammonites and that its teeth were specialized for breaking their shells.
